# A Portable, Active Abdominal Compression Binder for Orthostatic Intolerance: Design and Evaluation in Healthy Subjects

**Authors:** Vishnu S. Emani; Andreas Escher; Stephen P. Juraschek; Ellen T. Roche

**Affiliations:** 1Harvard University, Cambridge, MA, USA | 2Institute for Medical Engineering and Science, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA | 3Department of Cardiac Surgery, Boston Children’s Hospital, Cambridge, Boston, MA, USA | 4Wyss Institute for Biologically Inspired Engineering, Harvard University, Boston, MA, USA | 5Division of General Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA | 6Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 7Department of Mechanical Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA

## Abstract

Orthostatic intolerance is a category of disorders characterized by inadequate hemodynamic compensation upon standing. In this study, we developed a portable, active abdominal compression binder intended for individuals with orthostatic intolerance. We present proof-of-concept evidence in healthy volunteers demonstrating the binder’s ability to provide consistent abdominal compression, reduce tachycardic response upon standing, and maintain user comfort.

We designed and fabricated a novel active binder that applies motor-driven abdominal compression upon the detection of standing. Twenty healthy volunteers (ages 18–50 years) completed three randomized supine-to-standing trials: no binder, a commercial passive binder, and the novel active binder. Throughout each trial, compression pressure, heart rate, and respiration were continuously monitored and comfort was assessed via post-trial Likert-scale survey.

The active binder achieved a higher mean compression pressure (≈ 11 mmHg) with significantly lower intersubject variability (standard deviation (SD) ≈ 1 mmHg) than the passive binder (mean ≈ 8 mmHg; SD ≈ 3 mmHg). Active compression reduced the standing heart rate by 4.4 bpm compared to control (p < 0.05) vs. a 1 bpm reduction with the passive binder (p > 0.05). Neither the active nor the passive abdominal binders impeded respiration. Survey responses demonstrated that the active binder was at least as comfortable as the passive and was rated easier to don.

These findings suggest that active abdominal compression may serve as a more efficacious, consistent, and user-friendly alternative to passive binders for mitigating orthostatic intolerance.

Not applicable.

## Introduction

Orthostatic intolerance encompasses a spectrum of disorders characterized by an inability to maintain cerebral perfusion and stable blood pressure upon upright posture [1–3]. Under normal physiology, standing induces a rapid displacement of approximately 300–800 mL of blood into the abdomen and lower extremities, which in turn activates arterial baroreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid sinuses; these sensors trigger sympathetic vasoconstriction and an increase in heart rate to restore blood pressure and maintain cerebral perfusion [4]. When this baroreceptor-mediated feedback loop is compromised, whether through impaired mechanoreceptor sensitivity, autonomic neuropathy, or vascular stiffening, orthostatic intolerance may result [4, 5]. Clinically, this may present as postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), in which standing elicits an excessive heart rate increase of at least 30 bpm within 10 min without a marked drop in blood pressure [6] or as orthostatic hypotension (OH), defined by a fall in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure of at least 10 mmHg within 3 min of standing, potentially leading to dizziness, blurred vision, or syncope [4].

Orthostatic intolerance syndromes affect a significant portion of the population: POTS is estimated to afflict up to 0.5–1% of adults, predominantly young females [2, 7], and OH prevalence ranges from 5% for those under 50 years to over 30% among adults older than 70 years [4, 5]. Both disorders can lead to significant morbidity and reduced quality of life, underscoring the need for effective, user-friendly assistive strategies.

Current therapeutic strategies, including pharmacologic agents, functional electrical stimulation (FES), compression garments, and lifestyle modifications, offer partial relief from the symptoms of orthostatic intolerance syndromes but carry notable drawbacks. α-Adrenergic agonists (e.g., midodrine) and mineralocorticoids (e.g., fludrocortisone) raise systemic vascular resistance and blood volume, respectively, but are non-selective, often causing supine hypertension, paresthesia (tingling), pruritus (itching), and other side effects [1, 8, 9]. FES, involving lower body muscle electrical stimulation, can augment venous return via muscle contractions but demands clinical oversight and can discomfort patients [10, 11]. Compression garments, such as graduated stockings or abdominal binders, mechanically counteract venous pooling and thus increase standing blood pressure in OH patients [12, 13] and reduce tachycardia in POTS [12, 14]; however, these suffer from low patient adherence owing to difficulty donning, constant pressure discomfort, and inconsistent application [15, 16]. Additionally, leg compression stockings have been shown to be less effective in reducing the severity and duration of OH compared to abdominal binders and leg-to-waist stockings, as the abdomen contains a greater reserve of venous blood [17, 18]. Lifestyle measures (increased salt/water intake, physical counter-maneuvers) are generally adjunctive [17].

In recent years, there has been growing interest in abdominal compression systems that adapt to postural changes, with the goals of minimizing supine hypertension, easing discomfort when compression is unnecessary, and thus improving long-term adherence. Some designs entrust patients with manual activation, pulling straps or inflating bladders upon standing [19, 20]. However, these approaches depend on users physically engaging the mechanism and vary widely in ease of use. Other studies have explored fully automated compression methods, yet these prototypes often rely on bulky pneumatic pumps or slow-responding actuators that are not suited for portability and rapid on-demand compression triggering [21]. Additionally, there is minimal literature directly comparing the hemodynamic efficacy of adaptive abdominal compression systems against standard binders, nor assessing their relative comfort and usability profiles.

To address these limitations, we have designed a novel active abdominal compression binder that autonomously applies selective pressure to the abdomen during the transition to standing. The device aims to match the hemodynamic benefits of passive binders and maintain their lightweight, portable, and low-cost design, while enhancing comfort, ease of donning, and thus improve overall patient adherence and therapeutic effect. The active binder applies a target abdominal compression pressure of 11 mmHg via a motorized cord compression upon sensing upward rising motion. We evaluated the device in a cohort of 20 healthy subjects, assessing its ability to deliver consistent compression pressures, effectively attenuate orthostatic cardiovascular responses, and maintain patient comfort.

## Methods

### Active Compression Binder Design

#### Structural Layout

As shown in Fig. 1a, the active binder comprises two primary components: an incompressible felt base that encircles the torso, providing structural support and a surface for Velcro-based donning, and a thin fabric sheet forming a shortening region across the front abdomen. In the uncompressed active binder configuration, the circumferential length is 90 cm with a Velcro extender increasing the circumferential length up to 22 cm. The shortening region has a circumferential length of 16 cm, and the binder has a height of 20 cm. All rigid fixtures (motor housings, spool mounts, and string channels) were 3D-printed in polylactic acid (PLA) at 15–20% infill density, aimed to balance strength and weight. The entire active binder (including all electronic and motor components) weighs 0.29 kg. Figures 1b and c show the full active binder mounted on a mannequin before compression, and Fig. 1d shows the commercially available passive binder (Procare Health®, St. Peters, MO, USA).

#### Compression Mechanism

A single vertical column of metal grommets is positioned on each side of the shortening region. Four high-strength polyester cords are anchored to motor-driven spools. The loop configuration is shown in Fig. 1a: two strings loop through the central grommets and two loop through the peripheral grommets. Each cord’s single grommet pass minimizes friction and ensures even tensioning across the width of the binder. Multiple narrow fabric channels are sewn along the shortening region to guide the tensioning strings. When the user stands, the tightening cords draw the grommet columns together, reducing the shortening region’s length and thus increasing circumferential pressure applied to the abdomen.

Each cord reels onto a miniature spool, driven by a geared N20 micro-motor (100:1 gearbox, max 37 RPM; Greartisan Manufacturers®, USA). The motors and spools reside in a compact PLA fixture affixed to the felt base. From this housing, cords pass through the channels in the shortening region and then through their respective grommets.

#### Pressure Measurement

A bladder isolated from a brachial blood pressure cuff (11 × 20 cm) rests directly against the wearer’s abdomen, secured within a fabric pouch sewn onto the inner face of the shortening region. The bladder connects pneumatically to an HX710B pressure sensor (HiLetgo®, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China) on the outside of the felt. Uniform bladder compression by the shortened region yields real-time measurements of applied abdominal pressure.

#### Electronics and Sensor Configuration

All electronics are controlled by an Arduino Nano® micro-controller (Arduino, Turin, Italy). A lightweight 9 V LiPo rechargeable battery provides power; a step-down voltage regulator converts this to 6 V for the actuator motors, while the Arduino and sensor modules run at 5 V via the Nano’s onboard regulator.

Motor direction and braking are managed by a DRV8833 dual H-bridge driver (American Control Electronics®, South Beloit, IL, USA), interfaced to the Nano via 4 digital direction pins. The H-bridge supports bidirectional winding and rapid stops.

Binder activation is automated using an MPU6050 inertial measurement unit (IMU), integrating a three-axis accelerometer and three-axis gyroscope (HiLetgo®, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China). The IMU is mounted on the felt. A threshold-based algorithm running on the Nano detects the vertical acceleration during the standing event and commands the DRV8833 to wind the motors.

A single HX710B microelectromechanical pressure sensor measures abdominal compression via the embedded bladder. The sensor communicates with the Arduino over SPI at 100 millisecond intervals. Prior to deployment, we calibrated the HX710B against a laboratory-grade digital manometer, deriving a linear scale factor to convert raw voltage to mmHg. Calibration is only necessary during fabrication.

All modules, including the Arduino Nano, HX710B sensor breakout, DRV8833 driver, MPU6050, and power regulation circuitry, are consolidated onto a custom 4.5 × 6 cm printed circuit board (PCB) mounted on the felt base. The fully assembled electronics package weighs 65 g and operates untethered, supporting portable use when serial data logging is not required.

A closed-loop pressure control algorithm running on the Arduino Nano maintained a target compression of 11 mmHg. The firmware continuously detected peak and trough values over each respiratory cycle, computing the mean pressure from the previous breath. This mean was subtracted from the 11 mmHg setpoint to yield an error term, which was then scaled via a simple proportional gain to adjust motor winding. By updating only once per breathing cycle, this approach minimized overcorrection and conserved battery power.

With its 9 V, 600 mAh battery, the active binder can sustain over 3000 cycles of 10-s increase to max pressure and subsequent release, corresponding to sit-to-stand transitions.

### Passive Binder Adaptation

For comparison, a standard-grade, commercially available abdominal binder, which we call a “passive binder,” was modified to include pressure sensing (Fig. 1d). A second blood-pressure cuff bladder was positioned beneath the binder against the abdomen and secured via a sewn Velcro pouch. This bladder connected to an HX710B pressure sensor interfaced with an Arduino Nano, using the same SPI communication and calibration procedure described above. The electronics, including the Arduino Nano, HX710B sensor, and power regulation, were mounted in a portable enclosure, allowing for real-time monitoring of passive binder pressures during the study.

### Study Overview

To evaluate the consistency, effectiveness and comfort of the active binder, a randomized crossover study was conducted at the MIT Institute for Medical Engineering and Science (IMES) (IRB protocol #2503001596), in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. This study used a healthy-volunteer model consistent with prior work [22, 23], which assesses orthostatic tachycardic responses as a physiologic surrogate for venous return. All subjects provided written informed consent prior to participation. Figure 2 depicts the overall protocol flow.

Twenty healthy adults were enrolled; participants were eligible if they were in age range 18–50 years and had no known cardiovascular conditions, autonomic disorders, or standing difficulties. Table 1 summarizes the key characteristics of the study’s participant population.

After consent, each participant’s abdominal circumference was measured with a flexible tape measure following normal expiration. Subjects then completed three trials in randomized order—control (no binder), passive binder, and active binder—each consisting of 1-minute supine rest followed by 2 min of quiet standing. Heart rate and respiratory rate were continuously recorded via an ApneaLink Air™ (ResMed®, San Diego, California, USA) chest-belt respiration monitor and pulse oximeter. During passive binder trials, participants donned the binder and tightened it as per standard instructions for the device: “as tightly as possible.” In active binder trials, participants first adjusted the binder until it “just fit snugly,” then we verified fit by confirming a baseline pressure of ~ 2–3 mmHg; those with waist circumference > 80 cm used the Velcro extender for an appropriate initial fit. If the binder was not fit properly or the grommets were not vertically aligned (see Fig. 1a–c), the study personnel adjusted the Velcro attachment until alignment was corrected. All pressure and motion data from both the active and passive binder trials were streamed over USB via the Arduino Nano’s serial interface to a laptop and timestamped on receipt. We synchronized these timestamps with the ApneaLink Air chest-belt and pulse oximeter data streams. At any point, participants could manually disable the device by disconnecting an accessible power cord. The time between successive trial conditions within each participant was less than 2 min (for donning and preparation). At the end of the session, participants rated comfort and usability for each condition (Likert scale), given eight prompt questions.

### Statistical Analysis

Paired t-tests were used to compare mean compression pressures, standing heart rate, change in heart rate from supine to standing (ΔHR), and respiration rate between active, passive, and control conditions. An F-test was used to compare the standard deviation of compression pressures between active and passive binders. Multiple linear regressions were applied to evaluate the influences of abdominal circumference and sex on compression pressure, as well as to evaluate the independent effect of compression pressure and compression mechanism (active vs. passive) on heart rate responses. For all statistical tests, the threshold for significance was considered as p < 0.05.

## Results

### Compression Pressure

For all participants, the active binder reached its peak pressure in less than 7 s (mean 5.1 seconds, SD 1.23 s). Figure 3 summarizes the abdominal compression pressures achieved by the active and the passive binder under full tension, as well as the comparisons across sexes and baseline abdominal circumferences.

As shown in the gray boxplots in Fig. 3a, the active binder delivered a higher and more consistent pressure (mean 10.9, SD 1.3 mmHg) compared to the passive binder (mean 8.3, SD 2.86 mmHg) with statistical significance (paired t test p = 0.017, F-test p = 0.0013). This indicates that the active system not only exceeded the maximal compression achievable by the passive binder but did so with roughly half the variability across participants.

When stratified by sex, the active binder produced equivalent pressures for both males and females (mean 10.9 vs. 11.1 mmHg), whereas males fitted with the passive binder experienced higher average pressures than females (mean 10.3 vs. 8.3 mmHg). Further, the active binder maintained consistent compression regardless of abdominal size (linear regression p value = 0.29), while the passive binder showed a positive trend between abdominal circumference and applied abdominal pressure, whereby larger waists correlated with increased pressure (linear regression p value = 0.01) (Fig. 3b).

Multiple linear regression against passive binder pressure, as predicted by sex and abdominal circumference, demonstrated that abdominal circumference was associated with a significant increase in passive binder pressure regardless of sex (slope = 0.19 mmHg/cm, p = 0.02), but that sex did not demonstrate a significant influence on pressure when controlling for circumference (p = 0.29). Extensive regression results are shown in Supplementary Table 1.

### Heart Rate Response

#### Tachycardic Response Across Conditions

Figure 4a and b presents boxplots of ΔHR and standing HR for each condition: active binder, passive binder, and control (no binder). The active binder attenuated the increase most effectively (mean ΔHR = 10.8 bpm, standing HR = 69.0 bpm), followed by the passive binder (mean ΔHR = 12.8 bpm, standing HR = 72.0 bpm), and the control condition, which elicited the largest tachycardic response (mean ΔHR = 15.9 bpm, standing HR = 74.5 bpm). Medians follow the same order, indicating that the active device reduced the orthostatic heart rate surge relative to both passive binder and control.

#### Within-Participant Comparisons

Figure 4c (turquoise) depicts each subject’s pairwise differences in ΔHR: control vs. active (mean difference = 5.3 bpm, p = 0.0014), control vs. passive (mean = 3.3 bpm, p = 0.001), and passive vs. active (mean = 2.0 bpm, p = 0.098). The active and passive binders thus elicit significantly greater reductions in ΔHR compared to control, with a slightly greater effect demonstrated by the active binder.

Figure 4c (brown) shows pairwise differences in standing heart rate: control vs. active (mean difference = 5.5 bpm, p = 0.001), control vs. passive (mean = 3.3 bpm, p = 0.40), and passive vs. active (mean = 2.2 bpm, p = 0.01). The active binder thus reduces standing HR more effectively than either control or passive compression, the latter of which does not significantly lower standing HR from control.

Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2 demonstrate that the passive condition elevated both supine and standing heart rate relative to control conditions.

#### Heart Rate and Compression Pressure

Figure 5a plots each subject’s change in standing HR for active and passive trials against mean compression pressure, and Fig. 5b shows the ratios of standing HR to control over pressure. In the passive condition, the trend in both graphs suggests that higher passive compression pressures appear to correspond to smaller reductions in standing HR from control. However, the active binder appears to consistently outperform the passive binder at overlapping pressure levels, suggesting a potential independent effect of compression mode itself.

To quantify this, we performed a multiple linear regression on the standing heart rate reduction relative to control, using binder compression pressure and a binary indicator for condition (active = 1, passive = 0) as predictors. The model revealed a significant independent contribution of the active mechanism: the condition coefficient was 4.4 bpm (p = 0.005), indicating that, at the same applied pressure, the active binder yielded an additional 4.4 bpm reduction in standing HR compared to the passive binder. Similar findings were observed for the ratio outcome. Detailed regression coefficients and diagnostics are provided in Supplementary Table 2.

Supplementary Fig. 3 shows the relationship between control standing heart rate and passive pressure, demonstrating the importance of within-participant control comparisons.

### Respiration Rate

The data from the respiration sensor, shown in Supplementary Fig. 4, demonstrate that both active and passive devices appeared to have minimal effect on the breathing rate, differing from the control breathing rate by less than two breaths per minute on average. Paired t test analyses confirmed no significant difference (p > 0.05) in respiration rate between binder and control conditions in both the supine and standing postures.

### Survey Responses

Table 2 summarizes average ratings (1–5 Likert scale) across all participants for eight comfort-related statements for both binders. Overall, the active binder matched or exceeded passive binder performance on every prompt. The most pronounced differences were seen in supine comfort when no active compression was applied: the active binder scored 4.55 vs. 3.64 for the passive binder (p = 0.002), indicating that the active binder was significantly more comfortable when lying down. 80% of participants noted the active binder was equally or more comfortable than the passive binder while standing up (both binders under compression), and 100% of participants noted the active binder was equally or more comfortable than the passive binder while lying down (only passive binder under compression). Participants also found the active binder easier to don (4.36) than the passive (4.04, p = 0.09). Both binders were rated equally with respect to skin comfort (mean ≈ 4.8), suggesting no adverse contact effects in either condition.

Figure 6 shows the mean survey ratings for overall comfort, breathing ease, and skin comfort during standing under compression, with data binned into four binder-specific pressure quartiles. For both passive and active devices, overall comfort and breathing ease declined modestly as pressure increased, and this effect was most pronounced in the passive binder. In contrast, skin comfort remained consistently high (> 4 out of 5) for both binders across all pressure levels.

## Discussion

In this study, we demonstrated that a portable, motorized active abdominal binder can deliver precise, consistent compression pressures, resulting in attenuated orthostatic tachycardia in healthy subjects. The active binder maintained equivalent or improved user comfort and ease of donning across pressure ranges, addressing critical barriers to real-world adherence.

### Active Binder Design

In this pilot study of twenty healthy adults, our novel active abdominal binder design successfully meets its technical objectives of portability, minimal bulk, comfort, and rapid compression. While many traditional compression systems require stationary, external pump units and are unsuitable for ambulatory use, our device integrates all actuation and control components for portable use. The slim form factor and < 0.3 kg weight mitigate the risk that portability comes at the cost of increased wearer burden. As a point of reference, back braces commonly weigh approximately 0.3–0.4 kg, indicating that the device is in a reasonable weight range. The compact electronics system also eliminated the need for an external electronics pouch, a characteristic that other solutions require and may impede usability [21].

Beyond portability and lightness, our binder achieves its target pressure in under 7 seconds, significantly faster than existing pneumatic devices that can require up to 30 seconds to inflate [21]. Multiple studies have demonstrated that rapid onset of compression is likely critical for reducing orthostatic symptoms and countering the abrupt hemodynamic shifts that occur upon standing [24, 25]. Moreover, this fast-acting mechanism opens avenues for more advanced control strategies, such as intermittent or more advanced feedback-adaptive compression, which would be impractical with slower inflation systems. Should faster actuation be required in future iterations, the modular motor architecture allows straightforward upgrades: motors with higher RPM (at the expense of torque), additional winding spools, or optimized gear ratios could achieve the desired improvement.

The automated compression mechanism in our active binder, which detects the wearer’s transition to standing via the integrated IMU, offers hands-free operation and limits compression to moments of orthostatic stress. By engaging only when rising motion is sensed, the device avoids unnecessary abdominal pressure during periods of supine or seated rest, a significant advantage over patient-controlled inflation systems that rely on users to manually activate compression before each stand [19].

### Compression Pressure

Our results demonstrate that the active binder achieved a higher mean compression pressure than the maximum passive binder pressures, by around 2 mmHg (despite participants being instructed to “tighten as much as possible”) and did so with greater consistency. In the active system, pressure control software halts motor winding once the target is reached, whereas the passive binder reflects an individual’s maximal voluntary tightening. Consequently, if clinical needs dictate higher compression levels, the active device’s setpoint can be readily increased without hardware changes.

Variability analysis further underscores this advantage. The active binder exhibited roughly half the variability of the passive system according to standard deviation and IQR, indicating more consistent achievement of target pressure. Analyses revealed that, with the passive binder, males generated higher pressures than females and larger waists correlated with greater compression. It is important to note that sex and abdominal size are interdependent, and therefore the individual effects of each must be taken into consideration. The multiple linear regression suggested statistically significant differences based on abdominal size while keeping sex constant, but insignificant differences based on sex for a given abdominal size. Note that p-values are reported, instead of R2, because the question of interest is whether the slope should be considered nonzero. The result suggests that the sex-based variability in passive pressure observed may be attributed to differences in abdominal size, rather than sex independently.

In any case, this result is significant, as passive binders may be susceptible to greater variability; in real-world settings, factors such as age-related strength decline [15, 26] or reduced device familiarity could exacerbate inconsistency. Future work could investigate these factors in greater detail.

By contrast, the active binder’s closed-loop control and straightforward donning protocol minimize user-dependent variability. This consistency may be critical for predictable hemodynamic support across diverse patient populations.

The target compression pressure of approximately 11 mmHg was selected to balance hemodynamic efficacy with comfort and safety during sustained use. Prior studies have indicated that external abdominal pressures exceeding about 12 mmHg may become uncomfortable or unsafe for prolonged wear [27–29]. The higher pressures (20–40 mmHg) reported in the literature generally refer to internal bladder inflation pressures [20, 21], which have been shown to overestimate the true external compression experienced by the abdomen due to tension within the bladders [29]. In contrast, the present device applies compression through direct mechanical contraction, producing an accurately measured external pressure. Thus, despite differing nominal values, the effective abdominal compression achieved in this study is likely comparable to that of previously reported systems.

Previous work also suggests that the area of applied compression may be more influential for hemodynamic support than absolute pressure magnitude [30]. The active binder engaged most of the abdominal surface area, thereby providing effective coverage in this regard. Future work could systematically investigate how variations in compression force within the ~ 11 mmHg range influence hemodynamic response, to better define the optimal balance between efficacy and comfort.

The optimal duration for sustained abdominal compression also remains unknown. Prior studies have typically assessed responses over short intervals (≤ 3 min) [19, 20, 30], and longer-term physiological or comfort effects have not been systematically evaluated. In the absence of evidence supporting gradual decompression, the current device applies continuous pressure while standing to ensure stable hemodynamic support. The hemodynamic response to compression is likely patient-specific, varying with the degree of autonomic dysfunction and vascular tone. The active binder allows for individualized programming of pressure trajectories, enabling adjustments such as gradual pressure reduction or variable target pressures to optimize support for different patient profiles.

The design of the pressure measurement system also warrants further discussion. Our binder applies a flat pressure on the front of the abdomen, concentrating compression over the abdominal venous reservoir and minimizing pressure on the hips and ribs. The small pressure bladder, positioned directly beneath the flat compression region, was designed to measure local average pressure. Prior to testing, this design was evaluated in comparison with direct contact-based transducers, which yielded variable readings due to inconsistent apposition and shear. Additionally, since the same pressure measurement approach was used for both active and passive binders, relative comparisons are preserved even if a systematic bias exists.

### Physiological Efficacy

Our findings demonstrate that the active abdominal binder attenuates orthostatic tachycardia by ~ 5 bpm according to both ΔHR and standing HR. The passive binder achieves slightly less improvement, especially when examining the standing heart rate response. Although data on heart rate modulation in healthy cohorts are scarce, one prior study reported a 5–7 bpm decrease in standing tachycardia with a passive abdominal binder vs. no compression [23]. Discrepancies between their results and ours may stem from differences in donning protocols, investigator assistance during application, or participant demographics and physiology. Despite modest effect sizes in this healthy population, our data provide a compelling proof-of-concept that active abdominal compression can mitigate orthostatic heart rate surges.

The differing results between ΔHR and standing HR for the passive condition merit further consideration. The modest elevation in supine heart rate observed with the passive binder likely reflects slight sympathetic activation or discomfort during manual donning, which in turn may blunt its apparent efficacy at higher pressures (as seen in Fig. 5). Clinically, standing heart rate may be the more meaningful endpoint, since orthostatic intolerance is predominantly driven by blood pressure and preload demands rather than baseline variations in healthy individuals. Nonetheless, the active binder consistently lowered both ΔHR and standing HR relative to control.

Multiple linear regression demonstrated that the active mechanism provides an additional ~ 4.4 bpm reduction in standing heart rate beyond what pressure alone would predict. The results of the regression and the trends observed in Fig. 5 suggest a possible intrinsic advantage of the active mechanism beyond simply delivering higher pressures. One potential explanation is that continuous preload from a passive binder while supine may evoke parasympathetic compensation, blunting its efficacy upon standing [19, 31, 32]; the active binder, by only engaging during upright posture, may avoid this adjustment and therefore elicit more pronounced orthostatic support. However, given the paucity of prior comparative studies between passive and active binders and our modest sample size, this hypothesis remains preliminary. Future research with matched pressure setpoints between the active and passive conditions and larger cohorts will be needed to clarify the mechanistic underpinnings of active and passive compression.

Furthermore, it is reasonable to expect not only greater benefits of compression devices but also a more meaningful comparison of compression mechanism in patients with POTS or OH, whose baseline autonomic compensations are impaired, consistent with previous studies [14, 33, 34]. These results lay the groundwork for subsequent trials in clinical populations.

It is important to note that the clinical management of OH and POTS differs [35], and so implementation of this compression technology may be specific to patient populations. Despite these differences, compression therapy has been demonstrably effective at treating both OH and POTS [12], and the underlying mechanism (limiting splanchnic venous capacitance) has relevance for both pathologies.

### User Comfort

Survey data (Table 2) indicate that participants found the active binder at least as comfortable as the passive system across all eight prompts, with the most pronounced advantage noted during supine rest. As expected, higher compression pressures correlated with modest declines in comfort and breathing ease (Fig. 6), highlighting an inherent trade-off between hemodynamic support and wearability. Nevertheless, the active binder maintained comfort ratings equivalent to, or above, those of the passive device at each pressure level and, due to its programmable setpoints, offers the ability to finely tune this balance on a per-patient basis.

Ease of donning emerged as another crucial differentiator. Unlike the passive binder, which participants had to tighten manually under load, the active system only needs to be “snug” at baseline, after which motorized actuation delivers full compression. This simplified application not only drove higher ease-of-use scores (4.4 vs. 4.0) but also mitigates a major barrier to real-world adherence: difficulty putting on the garment. Poor adherence, reported at 30–50% for lower-limb compression stockings and even higher for abdominal binders, is attributed to both donning challenges and discomfort [12, 15, 36].

Many current approaches to adaptive abdominal compression rely on the user manually pulling straps or activating an inflation mechanism immediately before standing [19, 37]. These methods may further compromise usability and adherence, since they place the burden of timing and execution entirely on the wearer.

By allowing for automatic compression and donning at low tension, the active binder may have the potential to improve long-term compliance and broaden clinical adoption.

### Limitations

#### Device Limitations

The current prototype employs felt for the base layer, chosen for ease of fabrication but not optimized for long-term wear; future iterations could substitute minimally extensible foam or medical-grade padding to improve comfort. Although the test unit withstood over 200 compression cycles without failure, the cords, grommets, and fabric channels remain potential wear points. Future designs could incorporate low-friction nylon cords or pulley-based guides to reduce abrasion. More rigorous testing of device durability and battery life is required. The Velcro-mounted blood pressure bladder pouch was a temporary solution and replacing it with a permanently sealed, leak-resistant housing would reduce maintenance and prevent sensor displacement. The present prototype is not programmed for decompression upon sitting or activity (such as walking). Future iterations could include more advanced sensing and control to adjust or release pressure in response to posture or movement. Finally, the prototype lacks intuitive user-feedback features (e.g., LEDs or haptic alerts) to confirm proper donning, battery status, or component faults; adding simple interface elements will be crucial for independent use outside the laboratory.

#### Study Limitations

Since we enrolled only healthy adults with intact autonomic function, our results do not directly demonstrate efficacy in POTS or OH patients whose baroreflex sensitivity and vascular tone are compromised. While heart rate is generally a strong proxy for orthostatic stress, future studies should incorporate ambulatory blood pressure measurements or ultrasound-based assessments of venous return. The supine-to-standing transitions used here introduce variability in timing and effort; a tilt-table protocol could better standardize postural changes and enable exploration of intermediate angles. Although baseline supine HR differed minimally between conditions and trial order was randomized, hemodynamic effects during binder donning and potential cumulative effects across sessions could still have mildly influenced heart rate results. As compression pressure distribution can be influenced by differences in body habitus, future studies and design refinements will be necessary to address this potential variability. Comfort and usability ratings, while informative, are inherently subjective and may differ based on age, gender, or other factors; larger, more diverse cohorts and objective wearability metrics are needed to validate these findings. Future studies will require longer term, standardized safety evaluations.

## Conclusion

These findings suggest that active abdominal compression may serve as a more efficacious, consistent, and user-friendly alternative to passive binders for mitigating orthostatic intolerance. Our results support further development of such devices and their evaluation in larger clinical studies to investigate their physiologic effects in patients with orthostatic intolerance.
